scenarios.title: Connect a workstation using modified EUI-64
scenarios.summary: Build an IPv6 interface identifier from a supplied MAC, repair the next hop and verify the reply.
scenarios.objective: Address: Client/lan uses modified EUI-64 from the supplied MAC 06:25:96:ab:cd:ef inside 2001:db8:74::/64. Enter the full IPv6 address; keep /64 and mark the prefix on-link. Routing: Restore Client’s default path through the office router on lan. Verify the remote server 2001:db8:75::20 and its reply, as well as R1 at 2001:db8:74::1. Preservation: Keep every supplied interface address and prefix on R1 and Server. Do not replace their configuration to make an incorrect Client address appear correct.

guide.title: Understand the task
guide.why: The supplied MAC defines an identifier, while the /64 defines the office network. They serve different roles.
guide.action: Read the supplied address/routing requirements, then select Client. Use Addresses & interfaces for its derived full address and Static routes for its default next hop.

guide.title: Configure the address and route
guide.why: Toggling the bit and inserting ff:fe produce the interface half. A remote server still needs a real neighbouring router.
guide.action: Enter the derived address with /64 and on-link enabled. Repair Client’s ::/0 next hop on lan without changing R1 or Server.

guide.title: Verify both directions
guide.why: A plausible-looking identifier or a local-router reply alone is insufficient.
guide.action: Use Check configuration, then Inspect applied forwarding paths. Read which address, preservation or request/reply requirement needs attention and retry.

scenarios.explanation: The first MAC byte 06 has its 0x02 bit set, so toggling it gives 04. Inserting ff:fe produces 04:25:96:ff:fe:ab:cd:ef, grouped as 0425:96ff:feab:cdef. Attached to the supplied /64, Client uses 2001:db8:74:0:425:96ff:feab:cdef. A default route via the real office router on lan then reaches the server; the unchanged server route provides the reply.
hints: Keep the supplied /64 network half. The MAC determines only the final 64 bits of this explicitly MAC-derived address.
Six MAC bytes become eight identifier bytes by inserting ff:fe between bytes three and four. Then toggle the first byte’s 0x02 bit, including when that bit starts as 1.
After addressing, inspect Client’s ::/0 next hop. The configured fe80::99 is not the office router; use the actual neighbouring router on lan.
scenarios.simplifications: Explicit legacy modified EUI-64 arithmetic from a supplied nonzero unicast 48-bit MAC and canonical global/ULA /64. Native manual address/static-route editing and bounded request/reply forwarding; no MAC discovery, SLAAC/RA/ND/DAD packets, privacy-IID generation, real NIC, host commands or external networking. Modern hosts need not use MAC-derived IIDs. This is partial CCNA1.9.d and supporting1.8 practice, not full-objective coverage.

ipv6_teaching.prerequisite_note: Builds on IPv6 workstation addressing, /64 prefixes, link-local next hops and the native address/route editor. The introduction explains the additional hexadecimal-byte and bit-toggle ideas.

concepts.title: Separate the network half from the interface half
concepts.text: For the /64 used here, the first four IPv6 groups name the network and the final four identify an interface. A group holds four hexadecimal digits: 0–9 and a–f. Two digits make one byte (8 bits). A six-byte MAC contains 48 bits; this legacy method turns it into a 64-bit interface identifier.

concepts.title: Insert two bytes, then toggle one bit
concepts.text: Split the MAC after its third byte and insert ff:fe. Next invert the bit with value 2 (second from the right) in the first original byte. 0x02 means hexadecimal 02; XOR 02 flips only that bit. Toggle means 0 becomes 1 and 1 becomes 0: it does not mean always add 2. For example 00 becomes 02, while 0a becomes 08. The other seven identifier bytes stay in order.

concepts.title: Regroup and attach the supplied /64
concepts.text: Pair the eight resulting bytes into four IPv6 groups, then place those groups after the supplied network’s first four groups. Leading zeros may be omitted within a group. This changes the interface identifier, not the supplied network half. The worked table below shows every stage with separate practice values.

concepts.title: A correct address still needs a working route
concepts.text: An address inside the office /64 reaches local neighbours directly. A different network needs a route through the actual office router. Use its link-local address with the outgoing interface, or a reachable global address of the same neighbour. Check configuration verifies replies too; computing the interface identifier alone does not repair an unreachable default next hop.

concepts.title: Recognize the method without assuming every host uses it
concepts.text: This task explicitly chooses the legacy MAC-derived method. Many modern IPv6 interfaces use identifiers created without embedding a permanent MAC. Do not infer a device’s MAC or universal/local status from arbitrary IPv6 bits. Here you enter the address manually and test it in the simulated network.

ipv6_teaching.example_description: Practice values: Client MAC 00:16:3e:12:34:56; office prefix fd64:7::/64; server fd64:7:20::20. Build Client’s MAC-derived address and replace its unreachable default next hop. Keep R1 and Server addresses.
ipv6_teaching.try_change: After the worked repair passes, restore the original first MAC byte in the interface identifier and check again. Observe the specific bit-toggle feedback; a working route alone must not pass the address requirement.
